fit_paragraphs.text: Prof. van Schijndel's work on Hindi syntactic processing [paper:W4396913907] and on how contextual embeddings behave under orthographic noise [paper:W4402670872] connects directly to two problems I face in my research. My tokenizer adaptation work for Kannada showed that surface-level token fragmentation distorts model representations before any fine-tuning begins [lib:cv]; understanding the linguistic mechanisms behind that distortion is the next question I want to pursue. Prof. van Schijndel's approach—probing what embeddings actually encode about structure across languages—gives me a methodological framework for building evaluation beyond translated English benchmarks [lib:interests], which is central to my PhD research agenda.

Prof. Koenecke's investigation of speech-to-text hallucination harms [paper:W4391833135] addresses a failure mode I encountered in my own work: I trained a wav2vec2-style model on 40 hours of Tamil radio audio and observed that WER alone does not capture the kinds of errors that matter to users [lib:cv]. Her research on ASR bias and dialect disparities maps precisely onto the challenge of building reliable speech-text models for Indian languages where training data is sparse and primarily spoken rather than written [lib:interests]. I want to extend that line of inquiry to low-resource Dravidian languages where hallucination risks compound data scarcity.

Prof. Artzi's work on LLM evaluation methodology [paper:W4403346162] and in-context learning dynamics speaks to my second PhD research direction: building evaluations that measure what actually matters for multilingual users rather than proxy metrics on translated benchmarks [lib:interests]. My experience building a 2,400-sentence Tamil–English code-switched evaluation set—which exposed 18–26 point drops in open 7B models—gave me a concrete sense of how benchmark design shapes what we think models can do [lib:cv]. Prof. Artzi's emphasis on rigorous, task-grounded evaluation is the methodological foundation I want to develop further, extended to code-switching and cultural grounding in Indian-language settings [advisor:Yoav Artzi].

sop.text:
I am applying to the PhD program in Computer Science to work on multilingual natural language processing—specifically on making large language models useful for speakers of Indian languages who are poorly served by today's systems.

My interest is grounded in a concrete failure. In 2025, I built a Tamil–English code-switched evaluation set of 2,400 sentences and found that two open 7B models lost 18–26 points compared with monolingual Tamil inputs [lib:cv]. People in Chennai do not speak monolingual Tamil to a chatbot; they switch. That result became my first-author workshop paper [lib:cv] and convinced me that evaluation, not just training, is where multilingual NLP is broken [lib:interests].

At Microsoft Research India in summer 2026, I worked on the adaptation side of the problem [lib:cv]. Extending a SentencePiece vocabulary with 6,000 Kannada tokens cut average token count per sentence by 41% and improved downstream QA F1 by 3.4 points at the same fine-tuning budget [lib:cv]. The lesson was that cheap, targeted changes at the tokenizer level can matter as much as expensive fine-tuning—a result that now shapes how I think about parameter-efficient adaptation [lib:interests].

In a PhD I want to pursue three connected directions: (1) parameter-efficient and data-efficient adaptation of LLMs to low-resource Indian languages, including tokenizer design and data selection; (2) evaluation methodology that captures code-switching, cultural grounding, and faithfulness rather than translated English benchmarks; and (3) speech-text models for languages whose primary data is spoken rather than written [lib:interests]. In Spring 2026 I trained a wav2vec2-style model on 40 hours of Tamil radio audio, reaching 31% WER on a held-out set [lib:cv]—a starting point that made the limits of current architectures under data scarcity visible to me.

Three faculty at Cornell connect to these directions. Prof. van Schijndel's research on dependency locality in Hindi [paper:W4396913907] and on how contextual embeddings respond to orthographic noise [paper:W4402670872] offers a linguistic-evaluation framework I want to apply to tokenizer-induced representation distortions in Dravidian languages. Prof. Koenecke's work on speech-to-text hallucination harms [paper:W4391833135] addresses failure modes I observed in my own Tamil ASR project, and her research on dialect disparities in ASR maps directly onto the challenge of building reliable speech-text systems for low-resource Indian languages [lib:interests]. Prof. Artzi's work on in-context reinforcement learning in LLMs [paper:W4403346162] and his emphasis on rigorous LLM evaluation connect to my second research direction; I want to extend task-grounded evaluation methodology to code-switching and cultural grounding in Indian-language settings [advisor:Yoav Artzi].

I hold a CGPA of 9.21/10, placing me in the top 5% of my department [lib:profile]. I have a first-author workshop paper, two research mentors who have agreed to write letters [lib:recommenders], and experience as a teaching assistant for a 120-student machine learning course [lib:cv]. I organise the NIT Trichy NLP reading group, which has grown to roughly 25 members [lib:cv]. I expect to complete my B.Tech in May 2027 [lib:profile] and am ready to start a PhD in Fall 2027.

emails.subject: Prospective PhD student (Fall 2027) — multilingual NLP and tokenizer adaptation for Indian languages
emails.body:
Dear Prof. van Schijndel,

I am a final-year B.Tech student at NIT Tiruchirappalli applying to Cornell CS PhD programs for Fall 2027. My research focuses on evaluation and efficient adaptation of LLMs for Indian languages; I have a first-author workshop paper on Tamil–English code-switching evaluation and a summer internship at Microsoft Research India on Kannada tokenizer adaptation [lib:cv].

I read your 2024 paper "Does Dependency Locality Predict Non-canonical Word Order in Hindi?" [paper:W4396913907] with great interest. The question of whether structural locality pressures drive word order in Hindi connects to something I want to understand better: how tokenizer fragmentation of Dravidian scripts interacts with the structural representations models learn. I believe that combining your evaluation framework with my adaptation work could produce more principled multilingual benchmarks.

I would be grateful to know whether you are planning to take PhD students for Fall 2027. I am happy to share my CV and writing sample.

Thank you for your time.

Priya Raman

emails.subject: Prospective PhD student (Fall 2027) — speech-text models and ASR evaluation for low-resource Indian languages
emails.body:
Dear Prof. Koenecke,

I am a final-year B.Tech student at NIT Tiruchirappalli applying to Cornell CS for Fall 2027. My work spans Tamil–English code-switching evaluation and, more recently, training a wav2vec2-style model on 40 hours of Tamil radio audio—an experience that made the limits of WER as a metric very clear to me [lib:cv].

Your 2024 paper "Careless Whisper: Speech-to-Text Hallucination Harms" [paper:W4391833135] directly frames a problem I want to tackle: in Indian-language settings, data scarcity and dialect variation compound the hallucination risks you document, and the downstream harms in health and government information contexts can be severe [lib:interests]. I would like to extend that line of research to low-resource Dravidian languages.

Could you let me know whether you are planning to take PhD students for Fall 2027? I would be glad to send my CV at your convenience.

Thank you.

Priya Raman
